headline: Foggy, chilly mornings and dry afternoons today, then light rain arrives Saturday afternoon and evening, followed by a much stormier stretch next week with repeated rounds of rain, mountain snow, strong winds and a growing coastal-flood threat.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Friday starts cold and foggy: fog that formed in the Chehalis Valley is spreading north across the Puget Sound lowlands, with freezing fog likely in colder spots of the southwest interior and about a 55% chance of visibility under a mile at Sea-Tac between 4 and 10 AM. The fog should lift and break up by late morning or early afternoon, leaving a dry day under high pressure with highs in the mid to upper 40s inland and low 50s on the coast. Tonight brings another round of fog and freezing fog, though incoming high clouds should limit it mostly to the south interior around Olympia, with lows in the upper 20s to mid 30s.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: On Saturday a low-pressure system drops south from the northeast Pacific and parks offshore through Sunday, bringing rain to the coast by late Saturday morning and to the interior, including Puget Sound, by late afternoon. Amounts stay light through Sunday: only a few hundredths of an inch in the interior lowlands and around a tenth of an inch on the Central Coast. Snow levels hover near 2,000 feet, so the Cascade passes could pick up a light coating of snow (under an inch). Highs both days run in the mid 40s to low 50s.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Monday the offshore low is swept away as a larger, broad low-pressure system drops in from the Aleutians and deepens off the coast Monday night into Tuesday. That sets up an active pattern through the rest of the week, with several disturbances bringing multiple rounds of widespread lowland rain, mountain snow and gusty winds. Rivers will start to rise; no river flooding is expected at this point, but the Skokomish River will bear watching mid to late week.

coast: Calm on the water today, though fog may cover the inland waters this morning, with a 50–60% chance of visibility under 1 nautical mile on the Central and South Sound. Winds and seas pick up tonight: a Small Craft Advisory runs from 10 PM tonight into Saturday for the coastal waters and from 2 AM to 4 PM Saturday for the western Strait of Juan de Fuca, and a Gale Watch is up for the outer coastal waters Saturday morning and afternoon (50–70% chance of gales), with seas building to 10–13 feet by Sunday. A stronger system Monday into Tuesday is the bigger concern: gales are more than 70% likely on the coastal waters from late Monday morning, peaking early Tuesday with a 90%+ chance of gales and a 45–70% chance of storm-force winds offshore, plus a 50–70% chance of gales through the Strait of Juan de Fuca Tuesday and a 35–40% chance of an isolated storm-force gust in the Central and East Strait (the Port Angeles–Sequim stretch). Seas build toward 20 feet on the outer coast and stay above 10 feet midweek. High astronomical tides may bring minor coastal flooding to the Pacific Coast and Strait of Juan de Fuca by Sunday, and the coastal-flood threat grows Tuesday into Wednesday, especially on the Pacific Coast as large waves build.
watch_for: Freezing fog this morning and again Saturday morning in colder spots, mainly the southwest interior.
Tuesday's storm: possible storm-force gusts in the Central and East Strait of Juan de Fuca and on the outer coast.
Coastal flooding with high tides from Sunday into midweek, and the Skokomish River mid to late week.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in today's dry, foggy weather and the light weekend rain, and increasingly confident in a stormy Monday–Tuesday (90%+ odds of coastal gales), while the strongest winds and exact rain totals next week remain less certain.
